#4896. Can the BPC-157 ‘Wolverine’ Peptide Really Help With Pain and Recovery?

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Wellness seekers are increasingly turning to BPC-157, the wildly popular “Wolverine” peptide for injury recovery and pain relief, despite scant human evidence.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory panel voted in July to ease restrictions on it and several other peptides, recommending the injectable substances be made eligible for pharmacy compounding.

But before restrictions were eased, preliminary research suggests a rise in the use of the Wolverine peptide in recent years.

A September 2026 preprint analyzed more than 15 million medical records and identified 1,039 people with documented BPC-157 use.

The researchers found a roughly 33-fold increase in new users between 2020 and 2026.

The results, which were based on clinical records, have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

“The study found that BPC-157 use is largely hidden in clinical narrative rather than conventional prescription data,” said lead study author Venky Soundararajan, PhD, co-founder and Chief Scientific Officer of nference.

“The proportion of newly documented BPC-157 users who were male rose from 57% in 2020 to 70% in 2026, a statistically significant trend,” he told Healthline.

“The user population for BPC-157 peptide is increasingly male in proportion and increasingly younger with each passing year.”

BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide marketed and sold online for wellness.

Health claims about it and other peptides have spread on social media and in fitness circles and wellness communities, with high-profile advocates like Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. touting their benefits.

Proponents of BPC-157 claim the injectable peptide promotes injury recovery, pain relief, and tissue healing. Some advocates claim that “stacking” the Wolverine peptide, particularly with TB-500, may enhance its effects.

The “Wolverine” peptide got its nickname from claims that it facilitates rapid healing, echoing the regenerative abilities of the fictional X-Men character of the same name.

This promise of pain relief and recovery may be what gives the Wolverine peptide its appeal.

Soundararajan’s study found that nearly 33% of patients reported using BPC-157 for pain relief. By comparison, just 4% of patients reported using BPC-157 for performance enhancement.

Across the cohort of 1,039 patients, 27% reported improvements.

“Pain relief was the dominant reported benefit, documented in 183 patients,” Soundarajan said. “Wound or tissue healing was reported in 38 patients and functional return in 34 patients.”

“Part of BPC-157’s appeal appears to be to patients who remain symptomatic after chronic, complex or previously treated musculoskeletal problems, signaling a clear clinical unmet need,” he said.

Bert Mandelbaum, MD, a sports medicine specialist, orthopedic surgeon, and co-director of the Regenerative Orthobiologic Center at Cedars-Sinai Orthopaedics and Sports Medicine in Los Angeles, said that everyone experiences pain, but warned about the risks of using the Wolverine peptide to treat it.

“There is zero indication that BPC-157 has any efficacy for pain,” he told Healthline. “There’s zero evidence that shows that it’s good for clinical healing, and we don’t really understand the safety profile of it.”

Human evidence of the possible benefits and safety of the Wolverine peptide is limited.

A 2025 systematic review of current BPC-157 literature found that it was dominated by preclinical research and low-grade human evidence. The review authors said there was insufficient clinical safety data to determine the peptide’s risks.

A small 2021 retrospective study on the effects of injectable BPC-157 on knee pain suggests the peptide could help repair tissue and regrow cartilage. However, the study followed just 16 participants, lacked a control group, and did not assess impacts on function or quality of life.

An even smaller 2025 intravenous safety pilot on BPC-157 use involved 2 participants. While no adverse effects were reported during the short study, the researchers acknowledged that larger studies are needed to confirm safety.

The July 23–24 FDA advisory vote added BPC-157 to the Section 503A bulk drug substances list, allowing pharmacies to include it in compounded medications.

The FDA’s 8-6 vote, with one abstention, greenlit BPC-157 in both free-base and acetate forms.

The recommendation did not make BPC-157 an FDA-approved drug, nor is it a component of an approved product. The federal health agency has yet to make final regulatory decisions on peptides.

“RFK Jr. policies are hurting Americans,” Mandelbaum said.

“This decision is ridiculous. It’s another step in the wrong direction. There’s no basis for any of this stuff.”

The safety profile of the Wolverine peptide for use in humans is largely unknown.

As such, BPC-157 is banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency as an unapproved substance for athletes both in and out of competition.

The FDA notes that peptides like BPC-157 (free base) may be sensitive to product formulation, processing, environmental conditions, and impurities, which could degrade the products and reduce their effectiveness.

The health agency adds that it currently has limited safety information for how peptides like BPC-157 are administered.

Soundararajan explained that his study was unable to estimate the incidence or overall safety of BPC-157 because adverse events were captured retrospectively from routine clinical notes and are likely underreported.

“That said, the medical records examined contain both positive and negative patient experiences,” he said.

“Mood, sleep, skin, injection-site, and gastrointestinal symptoms are concrete safety outcomes among the few examined patient records with available evidence that deserve prospective measurement and discussions by healthcare providers with their patients who report using BPC-157.”

Some experts warn of short-term risks like infection at the injection site, but the long-term effects are not known.

“We don’t have publications of infections yet, but there are anecdotes of this,” Mandelbaum said.

“People are injecting their joints with this stuff, and you have no idea what it is. It’s not standardized. It’s not being regulated by the FDA, and I think people should recognize that. And although we haven’t proven it’s a safety hazard, we know it has no efficacy. So why do it? Why waste your money?”

Experts urge anyone considering BPC-157 or another peptide treatment to discuss it with their doctor first.

You might ask for evidence supporting its use, information on its quality, and whether there are alternatives with established safety and effectiveness profiles.

Mandelbaum noted there are many scientifically proven and safe alternatives to consider.

“We have spent the last 20 years developing an arsenal of biologics from PRP to bone marrow aspirate to adipose tissue to understanding glucosamine and hyaluronic acid,” he said. “We’ve done an amazing job at studying these things. We’re getting to the point where we are understanding the complexities of biologics. It’s exciting, and it’s impactful.”

Mandelbaum vehemently opposed the use of unapproved peptides like BPC-157.

He likened its rise in popularity to a “Ponzi scheme” promoted by “gym rats” and “internet influencers” who “leverage and exploit the gap between hope and knowledge.” Just because the FDA eased restrictions, he said, doesn’t make them any safer or more legitimate.

That said, any use of unapproved peptides should also be disclosed to a doctor.

“A short, open and empathetic clinical conversation can turn invisible consumer use of products like BPC-157 into useful clinical information that can critically help inform current and future care for such patients that ensure the best possible outcomes,” Soundararajan said.

BPC-157 should not be combined with other experimental peptides until research determines the potential for adverse reactions or events. Long-term use of BPC-157 and other peptides marketed for wellness is not advised.

#4895. Musk declares Tesla Robotaxi win over Waymo, but Waymo still drives 7x more

Elon Musk says Tesla’s Robotaxi race against Waymo “was never a real contest” after Tesla’s driverless fleet logged 438,000 miles in Austin in a single week, edging past Waymo’s 406,000 weekly average in the city.

That’s one city, one week, and a Waymo figure that’s four months old. Across the US, Waymo still drives about seven times more driverless miles than Tesla every week.

The chart going around comes from Robotaxi Tracker, a community project that pulls driverless mileage from each company’s own reports: Tesla’s weekly Robotaxi safety report and Waymo’s quarterly Safety Impact data hub.

Jason Scharf posted the Austin view on X with the comment that “the battle for Autonomous Austin might already be over.” Musk replied overnight: “It was never a real contest.”

The Austin data is real –albeit with some caveats. In the week ending October 18, Tesla reported 438,000 miles with no safety monitor aboard in Austin, up 30% from the week before. Waymo averaged about 406,000 miles a week in Austin in the second quarter.

But the tracker’s own caption explains the catch. Tesla’s figure is its latest week. Waymo’s is an average of April through June, because Waymo publishes about three months after each quarter ends. So Musk is comparing Tesla’s best week ever to Waymo’s spring.

Switch the same chart to “All markets” and the story flips.

Waymo averaged 3.90 million rider-only miles per week in Q2 2026. Tesla did 558,000 miles in its best week. Waymo’s Phoenix, Bay Area, and Los Angeles markets each drive more miles per week on their own than Tesla’s entire network.

Cumulative numbers are even more lopsided. Waymo has logged 271.3 million rider-only miles since 2020, including 50.7 million in Q2 alone, as we covered when Waymo released its latest safety data. Tesla has 3.11 million driverless miles since January 22, 2026. Waymo drove more than that in a single week.

And Tesla’s total leans almost entirely on one city:

Austin accounts for 79% of Tesla’s weekly driverless miles. Houston, Tampa, Orlando, and Miami combined did about 25,000 miles. Waymo’s smallest tracked market, Atlanta, averaged 250,000 a week in Q2.

The Austin surge has an obvious cause. Tesla launched public Cybercab rides in Austin on September 3.

According to Robotaxi Tracker’s count of the Texas DMV automated-vehicle list, Tesla now has 463 Cybercabs registered in Texas, 337 of them added in the last 30 days. That’s 48% of the 970 autonomous vehicles Tesla has registered in the state.

Tesla isn’t hiding the strategy. On the Q3 earnings call last week, Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s head of AI software, said the company wants to “swarm Austin with Cybercabs everywhere.” Musk said the Austin Cybercab fleet had grown “by a factor of 10” in about a month.

So Tesla dumped hundreds of new, company-owned cars into one metro and the miles went up. That’s fleet deployment. It doesn’t show the software can do what Waymo does in 15 cities, and Tesla can’t repeat it everywhere at once.

The bigger problem is what the cars are allowed to do.

On the same earnings call, Elluswamy described the service as constrained by the software, not by regulators. He said that if there’s “the slightest possible risk at all,” Tesla doesn’t take it on, and that the limits are “technology driven” for now. Service hours only recently stretched from 9 p.m. toward 2 a.m., and he listed highways, “higher speed roads,” 24/7 operation, and more weather conditions as things Tesla still has to unlock.

You can see those limits in the rides. Tesla Robotaxis don’t take highways, and riders report they avoid at-grade railroad crossings. In September, a rider had a 10-minute Cybercab trip in Austin turn into a 70-minute detour because the car drove south through East Austin until it found a bridge over the rail line, instead of taking MoPac.

That matters for this comparison, too. Miles is a flattering metric when your car takes the long way. A trip that should cover a few miles and instead loops across town logs a lot more mileage for the same rider.

Waymo, meanwhile, has been taking riders on freeways in Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles since November 2025.

Credit where it’s due: Tesla’s driverless miles are growing fast, 30% in a single week, and Austin now has a real Tesla fleet carrying the public without anyone in the driver’s seat. A year ago, that wasn’t the case.

I continue to hear tesla refer to its miles as 'driverless miles', but Waymo's as rider only miles. This can be a big difference. Are you sure that this is not an apples and oranges comparison? Do we have confidence that Tesla is only including miles with a rider inside and not driverless miles where the can is spinning circles in a parking lot??

But “never a real contest” is a strange thing to say when you’re behind by 7x on weekly miles and 87x on cumulative miles, and your one win depends on comparing your newest week to your rival’s data from last spring.

What stands out to us is the type of autonomy Tesla is deploying. In 2020, Musk wrote that “Waymo is impressive, but a highly specialized solution,” and that Tesla’s approach was “a general solution.” For years, Tesla fans dismissed Waymo as a geofenced system that only worked in mapped areas with lots of restrictions.

Now look at Tesla’s Robotaxi: geofenced, no highways, avoiding railroad crossings, taking 70 minutes for 10-minute trips, and limited by hours because the software isn’t ready for anything with “the slightest possible risk.” By Musk’s own old definition, that’s a highly specialized solution. Waymo is the one driving on freeways now.

#4893. Postpartum Prevention Plan: Time Outside, Exercise, Socialize

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 5, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Postpartum depression and anxiety are major issues that affect new caregivers. Many new parents focus on the birth plan to prepare for this major stage of life. But what I find in my work as a clinical psychologist is that new families really benefit from a postpartum plan as well. What are the needs, relationships, and activities that will help you maintain your well-being postpartum? Knowing these will promote your child’s well-being as well. I developed the following mnemonic to capture core helpful practices that are supported by research: Time Outside, Exercise, and Socialize. These three practices can provide a daily structure that maximizes joy during a time that is challenging but also fulfilling.

1. Time Outside: Follow the mantra often told to caregivers of newborns — leave the house every day. Time spent in nature has been associated with enhanced mood, emotional regulation, optimism, resilience, and child development (Hall et al., 2023). Research on mothers and nature has attested to the benefits of the outdoors on postnatal well-being and the relief it provides from indoor stressors (Hall et al., 2023). Getting out is key. Even if being in nature isn't possible, go out for coffee, lunch, or to a museum to provide novelty and stimulation that can vary your routine and perk up the day. Physicians have dispelled myths that you shouldn’t leave home with your newborn, as fresh air and a change of scenery are beneficial to both parent and child well-being (Davis, 2015).

2. Exercise: If you are able to, getting some kind of walk in every day with a newborn is not only good for you but also for your child. Strap them into a carrier of your choosing or affix a stroller with all the things you might need to leave the house for a stretch. A meta-analysis reviewing a wide range of studies found that exercise alone (without the use of other interventions) is effective in reducing postpartum depression and anxiety (Deprato et al., 2025). A moderate reduction in the severity of symptoms was achieved through at least 80 minutes a week of rigorous exercise, which could include a brisk walk, swimming, cycling, and other activities.

3. Socialize: Invite a friend or family member for a visit or walk. Attend a local baby-friendly gathering that can take you and an infant out into the world, like a yoga, music, play, or story time group. Research suggests that social interaction is a powerful protective factor in preventing postpartum depression and anxiety (Feinberg et al., 2022). Another study found that social support is particularly important for women who are at risk of postpartum mental health problems, such as those with more than one child, pregnancy loss, negative body image, and a history of mental health problems.

It is important to note that all three of these components overlap — socializing, time outside, and exercise could all take place during a long walk with a friend. But if you are having trouble getting out with the baby, have others help you, if possible, so you don’t have to make this happen on your own. And if consistent practice of these activities doesn’t seem to help, reaching out to a medical and/or mental health professional is essential. Severe cases of postpartum depression and anxiety may not remit with daily health behaviors, but require professional treatment, which can be very effective. More support is available at the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline (1-833-852-6262) and Postpartum Support International (1-800-944-4773).

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

Davis, S. (2015). Can I take my newborn outside? https://www.webmd.com/parenting/baby/features/can-i-take-my-newborn-outside

Deprato, A., Ruchat, S. M., Ali, M. U., Cai, C., Forte, M., Gierc, M., Meyer, S., Sjwed, T. N., Shirazi, S., Matenchuk, B. A., Jones, P. A. T., Sivak, A., & Davenport, M. H. (2025). Impact of postpartum physical activity on maternal depression and anxiety: A systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 59(8), 550–561. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2024-108478

Feinberg, E., Declercq, E., Lee, A., & Belanoff, C. (2022). The relationship between social support and postnatal anxiety and depression: Results from the Listening to Mothers in California survey. Women's Health Issues, 32(3), 251–260. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.whi.2022.01.005

Hall, K., Evans, J., Roberts, R., Brown, R., Barnes, C., & Turner, K. (2023). Mothers' accounts of the impact of being in nature on postnatal wellbeing: a focus group study. BMC Women's Health, 23(1), 32. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12905-023-02165-x

#4891. Increasing Ozempic Dose Linked to Lower Heart Risk Than Switching to Mounjaro

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Increasing the dose of Ozempic rather than switching to Mounjaro may be associated with a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), according to a 2026 insurance claims analysis presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting 2026 in Milan, Italy.

GLP-1 medications like semaglutide (Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro) have reshaped care for people with type 2 diabetes, but recent real-world evidence suggests these drugs may not offer identical heart protection.

It is important to keep in mind that this was a retrospective, observational study that showed an association, not causation.

More research is needed to fully compare the cardiovascular benefits of semaglutide versus tirzepatide.

The COMPETE SWITCH Cardiovascular (CV) analysis used Komodo Health’s Healthcare Map, a large US healthcare claims database with linked laboratory results, to examine real-world data from 636,525 adults with type 2 diabetes.

The analysis focused on 185,705 people who increased their semaglutide dose and 23,104 who switched to tirzepatide.

All participants included in the analysis were already receiving 1 mg of semaglutide (Ozempic) weekly.

The researchers found that people who increased their Ozempic dose to 2 mg had a 6% lower risk of MACE — including all-cause death, myocardial infarction (heart attack), and stroke — compared with those who switched to Mounjaro at doses up to 15 mg.

“This is an interesting study, but the findings may partly reflect medication adherence. When patients switch medications, it can take time to adjust the dose and find the right treatment level, which may temporarily affect how well their condition is controlled,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

He also noted that the study did not determine what might explain the difference in cardiovascular risk.

“It may be related to a combination of weight loss and direct effects on hormones involved in metabolism and appetite regulation,” Ali said.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are both GLP-1 medications. Ozempic (semaglutide) and Mounjaro (tirzepatide) are approved to help manage type 2 diabetes, while each medication also has a different brand approved for weight loss.

The semaglutide approved for weight loss in the U.S. is sold as Wegovy, and the tirzepatide approved for weight loss is sold as Zepbound.

“Semaglutide and tirzepatide work in a similar way. While semaglutide is a direct GLP-1 receptor agonist, tirzepatide is a dual agonist of both the GIP and GLP-1 receptors,” Amit Blumfield, MD, with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

“Because they work through somewhat different pathways, they can have different effects in individual patients,” added Ali.

While both semaglutide (Ozemipc) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro) work in similar ways, you may find that you tolerate one better than the other.

Ali noted that you should discuss any potential benefits and drawbacks with your healthcare professional.

“I would only recommend switching medications if there is an issue with tolerance of one or the other. If one medication is well-tolerated at increasingly higher doses and is effective in the desired weight-loss and blood sugar management, I wouldn’t necessarily switch,” added Blumfield.

These side effects are generally mild and may lessen over time. However, if side effects become difficult to tolerate, you should speak with your healthcare professional.

“GLP-1 medications can be highly effective for managing diabetes and promoting weight loss, but there is no one-size-fits-all treatment. The best medication depends on an individual’s health needs, goals, response to treatment, and potential side effects,” said Ali.

#4889. Korean police book 80 Tesla drivers over illegal FSD unlock devices

Seoul police have booked 80 people for using aftermarket devices to switch on Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving” in cars that aren’t allowed to run it in South Korea. Officers also seized 21 of the devices.

The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency announced the case on Tuesday. It’s the largest enforcement action yet against the FSD “jailbreak” hardware that has spread through China, Europe, and Korea over the past year.

Police say the suspects either imported the unlock modules from Europe and China or made their own. One plugged a European-made unit into his own Tesla. Another, an IT worker, built his device with information he found on GitHub.

Suspects also swapped advice online on how to unlock FSD and how to stop the car from keeping any record that it had been activated.

They’re charged under Korea’s Motor Vehicle Management Act, which bans unauthorized software changes that can affect a vehicle’s safety. The penalty is up to two years in prison or a fine of up to 20 million won (about $15,000).

The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport asked police to look into it back in April after finding signs of unauthorized activation. A police official told Korea JoongAng Daily that “safety risks were confirmed,” including the possibility of FSD misreading driving conditions. The investigation is ongoing, with police consulting the ministry and the Korea Transportation Safety Authority on the technical side.

Tesla launched FSD (Supervised) in South Korea in late 2025, but only on US-built vehicles: Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck. Those cars are exempt from Korean safety certification under the Korea-US free trade agreement. The Model 3 and Model Y, which Tesla ships to Korea from Giga Shanghai, haven’t cleared Korea’s safety standards for the feature.

And those two models are the bulk of the fleet. Citing Carisyou Data Lab, Korea JoongAng Daily reports that 47,458 of the 229,311 Teslas on Korean roads as of August, or 20.7%, can legally use FSD.

That number doesn’t match the government’s own count from a few months earlier. In May, data released by lawmaker Park Yong-gap showed just 4,292 of 180,684 registered Teslas (2.4%) were eligible: 2,708 Model X, 1,193 Model S, and 391 Cybertruck. Either way, the vast majority of Korean Tesla owners can’t legally use FSD, and some of them paid over $6,000 for it anyway.

The hardware is the same, which is why the hack works. The modules plug into the car’s CAN bus and get around the regional software lock.

Tesla has been fighting the devices itself. In April, it started remotely detecting them and stripping FSD from affected cars, warned owners they’d be fully liable for any crash and could lose warranty coverage, and permanently banned some Chinese owners from FSD.

Tesla & Starlink: The reality as reported in 2021: every one of our Tesla autos are connected 24/7/365 to the company. It was that year that a programming glitch came where some vehicles would not function. That was quickly corrected. In the news today where proof that when Elon shut down Starlink to Ukraine, russian missiles came and killed 5 people, including one baby. ... here is the reality you and me must face: Musk holds the power right now, that if he decides he does not like 'some owners' of Teslas, he can SHUT DOWN instantly those vehicles from moving. It is not enough that potentially, every conversation and communication device used inside those vehicles 'can' be recorded but, as he has proven perfectly willing to do to Ukraine families, so he could at any moment 'shut down' some specific users of Tesla vehicles at-will. this is not hype, fantasy or gusswork. This is how the online active update software communications system works on every car we buy from Tesla. My company is looking into other providers of Sat-Com services, and we are re-evaluating our own vehicle choices.

It’s easy to see why people do this. Picture a Korean owner of a Shanghai-built Model Y who paid for FSD, watching the Model X next door run the same software on the same computer. That’s frustrating.

Tesla sold FSD to owners of cars it had no regulatory path to enable in Korea, the same way it sold “Full Self-Driving” in Europe for years while approval kept slipping. It only dropped the name there this month after Germany pushed back. Sell a feature people can’t legally use and you create the market for the jailbreak.

Korea has now shown it will actually prosecute. So will Tesla refund the Korean owners who bought a feature their cars may never be allowed to run?

#4888. A Billion More Dark-Morning Commutes

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

In July, my post about the big debate over yearly time changes described the position of professional sleep organizations that permanent standard time (ST) is more aligned with our circadian physiology than permanent daylight saving time (DST), or the alternating system we currently have in the U.S. (except in Arizona). As a member of one of those organizations, and having read their arguments, I am in favor of permanent standard time.

Since I posted, an interesting study was released to journalists on October 29, which estimated the number of dark-morning student-commutes to school we would see if the “Sunshine Protection Act” (proposing permanent DST) had been passed by the Senate and signed into law. Rodríguez Ferrante and colleagues at the University of Washington calculated that the number was around a billion. Central to their argument against permanent DST was their analysis of a decade of national fatal crash records, which found that there were higher odds of pedestrian involvement in dark-morning crashes than light-morning ones (odds ratio [OR] 1.77), and even higher odds for children aged 5–18 (OR 2.22). Safety for children waiting for the bus and riding to school in buses and cars was a primary concern of some senators.

How have you and your family adjusted to this fall's time change? As for myself, after four days, I still get sleepy earlier in the evening and wake up earlier. I am in the “elderly” demographic, and it seems that with older age comes slower adjustment by the circadian clock (Lombardi, 2025). Lombardi explains that infants and older persons have a harder time adjusting to time changes, and the article also describes the physiology that makes adjustment difficult for many of us. Typically "spring foward" is more difficult for evening types (owls) than for morning types (larks), since they have to adjust to getting up earlier.

I came across an interesting fact in an American history book. It stated that “On Tuesday, October 30, 1787, readers of a newspaper, the New York Packet, found on the front page an advertisement for an almanac that came bound with tables predicting the 'Rising and Setting of the Sun,' the 'Judgement of the Weather,' the 'Length of Days and Nights’…” (Lepore, 2018, p.xi.). This was, of course, Ben Franklin’s Poor Richard’s Almanac. And while other almanacs with such information were available in early America, Franklin’s was the most read secular book of the time (the Bible was first overall). It is interesting to ponder what Franklin would have thought about changing the clocks and which of the three most discussed alternatives he might have supported. Among his inventions was a clock, and I have no doubt that he could have altered it to automatically adjust for yearly time changes.

Lepore, J. (2018). These truths: A history of the United States. New York/London. W.W. Norton & Co.

Lombardi, P. (2025, December 13). How Long Does It Take to Adjust to Daylight Savings? Biology Insights. https://biologyinsights.com/how-long-does-it-take-to-adjust-to-daylight-savings/

Rodríguez Ferrante et al., Over a billion more dark-morning school commutes for K–12 children under the Sunshine Protection Act, Current Biology (2026), in press. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.014

#4887. Oral GLP-1 Orforglipron (Foundayo) Achieves Weight Loss for Women of All Ages

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new GLP-1 pill called orforglipron (Foundayo) has been shown to help women lose weight, regardless of menopausal status, according to new research.

A group of researchers, including senior author Hunter Thomas Hoffman, PharmD, a clinical research scientist affiliated with the drug’s manufacturer, Eli Lilly, analyzed data from two prior trials, ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2, to arrive at this conclusion.

These studies reveal that this medication works equally well for women who have not yet gone through menopause, those who are currently experiencing it, and those who are postmenopausal.

The findings were presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD), held in Milan, Italy, from September 28 to October 2.

This is important because menopause often causes weight gain due to lower estrogen levels, making weight loss more difficult for many women.

Orforglipron offers a promising new option for managing weight in women with obesity or overweight, especially those with type 2 diabetes.

In April of this year, Eli Lilly’s Foundayo received FDA approval as a weight-loss drug, making it the second GLP-1 pill for weight loss to enter the U.S. market after Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy.

The ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 studies involved women who were either obese or overweight and who had at least one medical condition related to their weight.

Obesity was defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher, and overweight as a BMI of 27 or higher.

The participants were divided into groups based on their menopausal status: premenopausal (before menopause), perimenopausal (during the menopause transition), and postmenopausal (after menopause).

Each group included between 142 and 225 females who either received orforglipron or placebo, an inactive pill with none of the drug in it.

The ATTAIN-1 study focused on people who were overweight or obese but did not have diabetes. ATTAIN-2 included participants who had both overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes.

The purpose of analyzing these two groups separately was to understand how orforglipron works in people with different health conditions.

The researchers measured several outcomes over a period of 72 weeks. They examined changes in body weight, waist circumference (the distance around the waist), and the waist-to-height ratio, a measure used to assess body fat distribution.

They also tracked how many women reached specific weight loss goals, such as losing at least 5%, 10%, 15%, or 20% of their body weight, compared to those who took the inactive pill.

By studying these factors, the researchers were able to determine not only whether orforglipron helped women lose weight but also how much weight loss was achieved and how it affected their body shape.

The results showed that women who took orforglipron experienced significant weight loss regardless of their menopausal status.

In the ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 studies, premenopausal, perimenopausal, and postmenopausal women all lost an average of up to 14% of their body weight.

This means that the medication was effective for women at different life stages, including those experiencing menopause, when weight gain is often a challenge.

In addition to losing body weight, women in the orforglipron groups also saw meaningful reductions in waist circumference. Waist measurements decreased by up to 12.5 centimeters (about 5 inches) across all menopausal groups in both studies.

This reduction is important because greater visceral fat is associated with higher risks of heart disease and diabetes.

The waist-to-height ratio also improved for many women taking orforglipron. More participants treated with the medication moved into lower waist-to-height ratio categories than those who took the placebo.

This indicates a healthier distribution of body fat and suggests a lower risk of heart disease.

When looking at the number of women who reached specific weight loss milestones, orforglipron performed much better than the placebo. Up to 83% of women on orforglipron lost at least 5% of their body weight, while 30% of women on placebo reached that same level of weight loss.

Losing 5% or more of body weight is often considered clinically meaningful, as it can lead to improvements in blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol levels.

Overall, these findings suggest that orforglipron is a promising new medication for weight management in women with obesity or overweight, including those who also have type 2 diabetes.

This can be especially helpful for those navigating the challenges of menopause while trying to manage their weight.

James J. Chao, MD, FACS, Chief Medical Officer and co-founder of VedaNu Wellness, wasn’t involved in the research, but said the significance of these findings for postmenopausal women.

“The 14% is what’s grabbing headlines,” he told Healthline, “but up to 12.5 cm from the waistline is what I’m interested in.”

According to Chao, as females enter postmenopause, they tend to store more fat around their midsection.

“This is the type of fat that can cause heart disease,” he said. “So a pill that can help a 38-year-old woman lose the same amount as a 62-year-old breaks that myth.”

Additionally, in contrast to most GLP-1 drugs, which are injectable, it’s a once-a-day pill. You can also take it any time, Chao explained, making it more convenient.

“No needle, no refrigerator, and up to 83% of participants lost at least 5%,” he said. “Sometimes it’s the simple things that make a difference.”

Luca Moretti, MD, a medical doctor at Sapienza University of Rome, who wasn’t involved in the studies, added that convenience isn’t the only thing to consider when deciding whether to use orforglipron.

Obesity management should begin with an individualized plan that includes nutrition, physical activity, and the management of other risk factors.

“When these measures are not sufficient, adding pharmacological treatment can be considered together with a physician,” he told Healthline.

Moretti further advised speaking with your physician about any potential side effects, your existing medical conditions, other medications you are taking, and your treatment preferences.

“So the most useful question to ask a doctor is not simply, ‘Is Foundayo more convenient?’ but rather: ‘Among the available treatments, which one offers the best balance of effectiveness, tolerability, and practicality for me?'” he said.

#4886. Sykeruns X7 electric dirt bike review: A lot of power for surprisingly little money

The mini electric dirt bike market has exploded over the last few years, with seemingly countless new brands offering everything from pint-sized electric pit bikes to surprisingly powerful off-road machines. The Sykeruns X7 falls somewhere in the middle, offering enough power to get into some serious trouble while keeping the price relatively approachable.

I’ve spent some time now riding the X7, and while it certainly isn’t the most refined electric dirt bike I’ve tested, there’s enough to like about what you’re getting for the money.

In fact, if you’re looking for a reasonably powerful electric dirt bike for recreational trail riding without spending several thousand dollars, this might be worth a closer look.

The Sykeruns X7 is a compact electric dirt bike featuring a 5,500W peak-rated motor, which translates to around 7.4 horsepower. That’s quite a bit of power for a bike at this price point of $1,699, especially considering that many similarly priced electric two-wheelers are significantly less powerful. Oh, and for our readers, we’ve gotten you set up with a 20% discount. Just use code ELECTREK20 to drop the price down to an impressive $1,359!

Sykeruns claims a top speed of 57 mph (92 km/h), though since this is an off-road only bike, you’ll rarely get the chance to put that claim to the test. I certainly didn’t, as I didn’t have a long enough and flat enough stretch of trail where I felt comfortable hitting nearly highway speeds on a low-cost e-moto.

The battery is a 60V 27Ah pack, providing 1,620 Wh of capacity. Sykeruns claims up to 60 miles (96 km) of range, though as with virtually every electric dirt bike, your actual range will depend heavily on how aggressively you’re riding. Fast trail riding, steep climbs, and repeated hard acceleration can eat through battery capacity much more quickly than leisurely cruising. Suffice it to say that you’ll likely not see the 60 mile figure in real world scenarios, but that’s still a fairly large battery.

The bike rolls on a 17-inch front wheel and 14-inch rear wheel, both wrapped in knobby off-road tires. Hydraulic disc brakes handle stopping duties, while an inverted suspension fork and rear monoshock help smooth out the bumps.

At 143 lb (65 kg), the X7 isn’t exactly featherweight, but it’s also far from being a full-size electric motorcycle.

The first thing I was surprised about with the X7 is that it offers a pretty decent amount of performance for the money. There’s enough power here to have some real fun, and the bike doesn’t feel like one of those underpowered mini electric motorcycles that struggles once you get beyond casual neighborhood speeds.

That said, I wouldn’t describe the acceleration as mind-blowing, either. We’re not talking about the kind of explosive power delivery you’d get from a high-end electric dirt bike costing several times as much. Instead, the X7 delivers a healthy amount of acceleration that feels appropriate for a recreational off-road machine.

And let’s be real here, that’s probably what most people shopping in this budget category are looking for.

The suspension is another area where the X7 earns a passing grade without necessarily winning any awards. The front fork and rear shock do their jobs, absorbing the bumps and ruts you’d expect to encounter on typical trails. It’s nothing I’d call plush, but I could see it doing light jumps with minimal air time.

Would I want to take this thing to a motocross track and start launching it off massive jumps? Not particularly. The suspension doesn’t have the premium feel or sophisticated damping of more expensive machines.

But for general trail riding, exploring dirt roads, and the occasional overlanding shenanigans, it’s perfectly serviceable. Not every electric dirt bike needs to be a competition-ready machine, and the X7 seems comfortable occupying that more recreational category.

I was also pleasantly surprised by the tires, which seem well suited to the bike’s intended purpose. The knobby tread offers a reasonable amount of grip for off-road riding, and I didn’t find myself immediately wishing for a tire upgrade.

The overall size is worth mentioning, too. This isn’t a particularly large electric dirt bike, but at my modest 5’7” (170 cm) height, I felt comfortable on it. The riding position didn’t feel overly cramped, and the bike was manageable enough that I didn’t feel like I was wrestling with an oversized machine.

Taller riders might find it a bit more compact than they’d prefer, but for average-height riders, the proportions seem reasonable.

If there’s one area where the X7 reminds you of its budget-friendly $1,699 price tag, it’s the overall level of refinement.

Nothing about the bike struck me as particularly premium. The components, finishes, and general construction are more in line with what I’d expect from a relatively inexpensive electric dirt bike.

But that’s not necessarily a criticism. There’s a difference between something feeling inexpensive and something feeling inadequate, and the X7 generally stays on the acceptable side of that line.

The controls are straightforward, the digital display provides the basic information you need, and the overall package feels focused on delivering usable performance rather than impressing riders with fancy features.

The grippy hydraulic brakes are also a welcome inclusion, especially considering the speeds this bike is capable of reaching. With a machine that can approach highway speeds, having proper motorcycle-style braking hardware is important.

Of course, long-term durability is a separate question. Budget electric dirt bikes don’t always have the same track record, parts availability, or established dealer networks as the more recognizable motorcycle brands. That’s something worth considering before purchasing, particularly if you plan to ride hard or frequently.

One thing I appreciate about the Sykeruns X7 is that the company makes its intended use fairly clear.

There’s a large red warning sticker on the bike explaining that it’s intended for off-road use only. That’s a good thing, especially in today’s market, where the lines between electric bicycles, electric dirt bikes, and electric motorcycles are becoming increasingly blurred, despite laws existing to keep these types of bikes out of the bike lane and off of public roads.

The X7 is absolutely not an electric bicycle. It doesn’t have pedals, it produces several thousand watts of power, and it’s capable of speeds far beyond anything permitted under electric bicycle regulations.

It’s an off-road electric motorcycle, plain and simple.

Interestingly, though, Sykeruns has equipped the bike with features like a tail light and turn signals, which could potentially give some riders the wrong impression.

Those are certainly useful features on a motorcycle, but they don’t magically make a vehicle street legal. Without the necessary certification, registration, and other road-use requirements, the X7 remains an off-road-only machine.

I worry that some buyers might see those lights and assume they can ride the bike around town like a small electric motorcycle. That’s not the case, and it’s important to understand that distinction before buying one.

After spending time with the Sykeruns X7, my biggest takeaway is that this is a reasonably capable electric dirt bike at a pretty compelling price.

It’s not the best electric dirt bike I’ve ever ridden. The suspension is fairly basic, the build quality is unremarkable, and there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about the design.

But for $1,699 (or $1,359 if you use the code ELECTREK20 to take 20% off!), you’re getting a 5.5 kW peak-rated electric motorcycle with a sizable battery, proper off-road tires, hydraulic brakes, and enough performance to have some genuine fun on the trails.

I wouldn’t say that the X7 here is trying to compete with more up-market electric dirt bikes from the likes of Juiced, Sur-Ron or Talaria on overall refinement, but they make this type of riding much more accessible.

And that’s really where I think the X7 makes the most sense.

If you’re an experienced dirt bike rider looking for a highly refined machine with excellent suspension and premium components, you’ll probably want to keep shopping.

But if you’re someone who wants a fun electric dirt bike for exploring private property, cruising around trails where motorized riding is permitted, or just enjoying some recreational off-road riding without spending a fortune, the Sykeruns X7 offers a pretty reasonable package.

It doesn’t need to be amazing at everything. At this price, being pretty good at most things is already an accomplishment.

#4883. A Fun Way to Build Relational Skills

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 5, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Our relationships are the source of some of our greatest joys and deepest pain. When our relationships are thriving, we tend to thrive, and when they’re strained, we suffer. In fact, many of the most pressing problems, not only in our personal lives but also in the larger world, such as interpersonal abuse, war, racism, climate change, and animal exploitation, are driven by dysfunctional ways of relating: to other people, to animals and the environment, and even to ourselves. So building relational literacy—the understanding of and ability to practice healthy ways of relating—can help transform these problems.

Yet the people who most need to build relational literacy are also probably the least likely to pick up a self-help book or go to therapy. They may, however, happily spend an evening engrossed in a novel or bingeing on Netflix.

What if we could build relational skills through reading or watching enjoyable stories?

Stories, whether written or on-screen, teach us things, from how a courtroom works to what healthy communication looks like. Research suggests that stories also shape our beliefs and attitudes, for better or worse. And because every story features characters, and characters are always relating—to others, and at the very least to themselves—every story is teaching us how to relate. The only question is whether we’re learning skillful or harmful ways of relating.

Consider the all-too-common bar scene in which an affronted man “communicates with his fists” by beating up a stranger who was making eyes at his partner. Or the many revenge movies in which an aggrieved parent (often a father) seeks not only to catch, but to brutalize, the person who kidnapped their child. In contrast, series like This Is Us portray complex relationships and characters who are nuanced and vulnerable, who turn toward rather than against or away from each other, and who repair after a relational breach.

Stories can also help us recognize difficult-to-identify dynamics, such as those that arise with addiction or domestic abuse. We often see more clearly when we look at a situation from the outside, as observers of someone else’s experience. For example, the film When a Man Loves a Woman reveals how alcohol dependence impacts a family system, while the novel and movie It Ends With Us reveal how gaslighting and trauma bonding operate in an abusive relationship.

If you’re building relational skills through such means as reading nonfiction or taking courses, fiction can be a powerful supplement. Stories can bring the principles and tools described in nonfiction to life, showing what they look like and how they can be applied. This is why, after writing seven nonfiction books, several of which are about relationships, I wrote a novel. I wanted readers to be able to see relational concepts in action while also being entertained.

To get more out of novels and shows as tools for relational learning, you can use a list of questions for post-reading or -viewing. You can tailor the list to areas you want to grow in or concepts you’re learning through therapy or nonfiction (for example, attachment styles, relational repair, or the Gottmans’ “four horsemen”), and use it for personal reflection or for discussion with someone you’ve read or watched with.

You can start with questions like the following:

I’ve always believed that a great story leaves the reader or viewer a little better off than they were before. Whether you’re a therapist working with clients or an individual wanting to build your relational skills, consider adding stories to your relational toolkit. Stories not only teach us; they can help us have fun in the process of learning.

Braddock, K., & Dillard, J. P. (2016). Meta-analytic evidence for the persuasive effect of narratives on beliefs, attitudes, intentions, and behaviors. Communication Monographs, 83(4), 446-467.

Hermann, E., Morgan, M., & Shanahan, J. (2021). Television, continuity, and change: A meta-analysis of five decades of cultivation research. Journal of Communication, 71(4), 515-544.

Joy, M. (2025). A half-hearted death wish. Two Steps Forward Press.

Joy, M. (2023). How to end injustice everywhere: Understanding the common denominator driving all injustices, to create a better world for humans, animals, and the planet. Lantern Publishing & Media.

#4882. This Is Not Your Ordinary Flu Season

The CDC released new data that changes what to expect this season.

EVERY FLU SEASON is different. Some come earlier, others later. Some are mild, while others—like last year—barrel through like a tornado. Every year, scientists do their best to predict what type of influenza virus will hit the US based on data from countries in the Southern Hemisphere whose flu seasons come earlier than ours.

The key word here is predict. Since the influenza virus mutates quickly, it’s hard for scientists to give a 100 percent guarantee that what’s ravaging Australia will also come for the US. That’s what happened in the brutal flu season last year—and this year.

A few weeks ago, scientists gave a forecast of H3N2 (that’s the one dubbed “Super-K”) as the dominant flu strain for the US. But early surveillance in flu cases from the West Coast found that a different type—Influenza A virus subtype H1N1—has overtaken H3N2 as the dominant flu strain in October. The CDC also released new flu data reporting a spike in flu-related hospitalizations.

Does H1N1 sound eerily familiar? H1N1 is also known as swine flu—a strain that sparked a pandemic back in 2009. So far, researchers have linked early flu ER visits to a mutation in H1N1 (a G155E mutation) that changes the way the virus attaches to and infects cells. Past research has found antibodies from past H1N1 infections or vaccinations may not recognize it, especially in younger populations. In other words, there is a chance the mutated influenza virus could evade some pre-existing immunity.

Here is what you need to know about this early jump to flu season and how to best protect yourself against this mutated strain.

HERE’S WHAT THE CDC learned: In mid-October this year, the agency saw 10 times more hospitalizations for flu than it did in 2025 (2.1 hospitalizations per 100,000 people compared to 0.2 per 100,000 during the same week last year).

Among other changes are when and where the virus is spreading. While influenza cases typically tick up around fall, infections began rising in August. The boost of early cases was mostly on the West Coast, including Arizona, Nevada, and California. Hawaii and Louisiana are already at moderate levels. Typically, the US flu season starts in the South.

Flu activity remains low nationally. But as of October 28, the CDC estimates that infections are growing or likely growing in 39 states. The numbers coincide with early reports of flu activity ramping up on the East Coast in states including Pennsylvania and New York.

WHILE SCIENTISTS INITIALLY predicted a “Super-K” flu strain to be dominant, this year’s vaccine accounts for multiple flu strains. The current flu shots will target three strains: H1N1, B/Victoria lineage, and H3N2. It’s too soon to see if the vaccine will fully protect against the mutated H1N1 strain, but it’s still expected to provide some meaningful protection.

“A mismatch is not a black-or-white situation. We may have less immunity, not no immunity,” Andrew Pekosz, PhD, virologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health told TODAY.com. You can also take some reassurance from last year when people who still got the mismatched flu shot were still less likely to have severe illness and be hospitalized than those who were unvaccinated.

ALONG WITH YOUR traditional flu shot, adults ages 50 and over are eligible for a new flu vaccine called mFLUSIVA made with the same mRNA technology as the COVID vaccines. A phase 3 clinical trial on the mFLUSIVA vaccine found it was more effective at preventing illness from influenza virus subtypes A and B than a standard vaccine. Reminder, the dominant strain right now is Influenza A virus subtype H1N1.

Of the 20,179 people injected with the new shot, only 411 developed a lab-confirmed case (2 percent) 14 days after vaccination during flu season last year. Meanwhile, 557 of 20,124 recipients of the standard vaccine got sick with the flu (2.8 percent).

One caveat, however, was that the new flu vaccine has a greater chance of severe side effects. In the clinical trial, people were more likely to report injection site pain, fatigue, headaches, and muscle weakness.

Don’t want a shot? That’s fine! You also have your choice of a nasal flu vaccine a.k.a. FluMist if you’re ages 2 to 49. “We tend to develop less of an immune response in the nose as we get older, which means the nasal spray vaccine doesn’t work as well in older groups,” John Sellick, DO, infectious disease expert and professor of medicine at the University at Buffalo, previously told MH.

Ultimately, time isn’t running out yet to get yourself armed and ready for the US flu season. The influenza virus is fast and mutates easily, but vaccination remains your best option to weather the storm.

Jocelyn Solis-Moreira, MS is the associate health & fitness for Men's Health and has previously written for CNN, Scientific American, Popular Science, and National Geographic before joining the brand. When she's not working, she's doing circus arts or working towards the perfect pull-up.

#4881. Switching from GLP-1 Injections to Wegovy Pill Shows Additional Weight Loss of 4.1%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People with overweight or obesity who switch from an injectable GLP-1 medication to the Wegovy (semaglutide) pill may continue to lose weight, according to findings from the OCTANE study presented at the 2026 Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy.

The study is among the first real-world analyses to examine weight loss and treatment experiences among people who switched from an injectable weight loss medication to oral semaglutide (Wegovy).

However, while real-world studies like this can provide useful insights into how treatments work in everyday life, these findings do not prove that switching to the Wegovy pill caused the weight loss.

The results have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

This was a retrospective cohort analysis evaluating weight change, treatment adherence, and patient satisfaction after people switched from injectable semaglutide (Wegovy) or tirzepatide (Zepbound) to oral semaglutide for weight management.

The study included a random sample of 194 adults with overweight or obesity and at least one obesity-related complication, such as hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnea, and dyslipidemia.

Participants had no history of diabetes or bariatric surgery and had an average baseline weight of 221.6 pounds (100.5 kg) and an average body mass index (BMI) of 34.5 kg/m2.

Participants switched from an injectable GLP-1 medication to oral semaglutide between January 5 and February 7, 2026. There was no requirement for how long they had used an injectable medication or how much weight they had lost before switching.

Participants were required to use oral semaglutide regularly for 3 months and self-report their weight within 30 days of starting treatment and again at the end of the study period.

After 3 months of taking oral semaglutide, participants had lost an average of 4.1% of their body weight, or 8.8 pounds.

At the 3-month mark, 2 in 5 participants (40.7%) had lost 5% or more of their body weight.

The proportion of participants with a BMI of 30 or greater also decreased by 21.6 percentage points, from 87.1% at baseline to 65.5% after 3 months.

Most participants (82.4%) reported at least one treatment improvement. Around 69% reported better-fitting clothes, and around 51% reported eating healthier.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Medical Director, Diabetes & Metabolic Center at University Hospitals, Cleveland, OH, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that, “These findings are encouraging because they suggest that some people can continue losing weight after switching to oral treatment.”

However, she also noted, “I would view this as promising early evidence supporting another treatment option, rather than proof that switching improves results.”

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, noted that because the oral medication is absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract, less of it reaches the bloodstream compared to the injectable form.

However, oral semaglutide can still be effective for weight loss.

“While studies show that the injectable form is more efficacious, current findings demonstrate that the oral version is also effective for weight loss,” said Ali.

Some people may prefer the oral form for ease of use and transportation because it does not require refrigeration. However, it must be taken in the morning on an empty stomach, followed by a 30-minute wait before eating, Ali told Healthline.

“Both formulations can cause gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation. Taking a pill does not eliminate those risks,” Hatipoglu said.

Hatipoglu also said factors to consider include how well your current treatment is working, side effects, your comfort with injections, your daily routine, cost, and insurance coverage.

She added that the decision should be made with a prescribing clinician, who can help plan the transition and monitor your response.

“Both options can be effective, so patients should discuss the risks and benefits of each with their provider. Ultimately, these medications are tools to support a healthier diet and lifestyle, and patients who make these fundamental changes achieve the best results,” said Ali.

#4879. Forget These 4 Ab Workout Myths. Train Using These Principles Instead.

Know the truth before you begin your transformation.

YOU WANT TO get in shape, and you want to look the part. So you tack on some extra time to the end of your workout to hit your abs, sure that those extra crunches will result in a six-pack sooner than later. Right?

Before we go any further, there are a handful of notions about your core training that you need to ditch immediately. If any of these sound familiar to you, don’t sweat it. You’ve likely heard about thousands of ab-building techniques, and it’s no easy feat to sift through all that information in search of the truth. What’s important is understanding what ab results are possible through consistent training. This will save you during those moments five weeks into this program when you’re questioning if you should keep going. You’ll remember what the process is, why it works, and why you really do have to log that day’s sets.

I can’t stress this enough: the abs should be treated no differently than other muscles in the body. A muscle is a muscle, and that means three things: muscles don’t work independently, muscles adapt to resistance training, and muscles need appropriate recovery to develop.

Unfortunately, when you have a topic like abs, which are arguably the most Googled and sought-after body part, you will get a large mix of opinions on how to approach training. The approach I want you to take with me as your coach is the science-based one. We aren’t going to live in the anecdotal world of “my one friend did this and got great results.” When it comes to exercise, there isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution, but there are some tried-and-true facts we have learned over the years with science and research. These are the key principles I share with my clients when it comes to breaking down the misinformation about abs.

I AM NOT sure when this myth started, but for some reason people are under the impression that abs are uniquely different from other muscles in that you can train them every day. That is absolutely not true.

Overuse of any muscle actually leads to atrophy (deterioration) of the muscle, which is the exact opposite of what you want when you are trying to build your abs. When it comes to core training and core conditioning, it’s more effective to have a mix of higher and lower intensity days, as you’ll see later in the program.

Going all out is an outdated approach to training. You simply can’t go full throttle every day and expect to stay on the ball throughout the program. There are a handful of people in the world who can do just that, and that’s amazing. But we can’t create a workout plan based on outliers. It needs to be based on general outcomes. So, in order to give yourself appropriate recovery time, challenge your muscles in different ways, and ensure continued success, it’s best to navigate between different intensity days.

THERE IS NO such thing as spot reduction.

Direct abdominal work isn’t going to burn off that layer of fat laying on top of your abs the way you might hope. Burning fat is much better attacked through nutrition, strength training, and cardiovascular exercise. The best approach is a holistic one, like I’ve designed for you in this plan.

The way you develop your core in this program will change the way you look at training moving forward. By mixing up exercises and taking a step-by-step approach to building up a strong core, you’ll see changes in everything from the way you look to the way you feel to the way you move through your day! These 90 days will build you up from the inside out into the strongest version of yourself.

BELIEVE IT OR not, they can be the same. That is the basis of this program—to blend ability with visibility.

You shouldn’t feel doomed to endless days of crunches wondering why the results just aren’t coming to you. Variety and emphasis will be large determining factors of your training. With the right mix, you will be able to get the look you want with the function you need.

HAVE YOU EVER noticed two people with differently shaped abs? Maybe one person’s abs are deeper, more symmetrical, and more defined than his buddy’s. I mean, Arnold Schwarzenegger is famous for having four visible abs no matter how shredded he got. Why is that?

Well, that is something you are born with. Thick cords of fibrous tissue stretch across the abdominal wall. The main connective tissue that runs down the center of the abdomen is called the linea alba. That line can be straight or slightly angled, depending on your genetics, and determines how symmetrical your abs appear to be. How many of the crossing tendinous fibers you have (which can be three or more) determines what kind of pack you can get, be it a six-pack, eight-pack, or even a 10-pack.

#4878. Waymo adds nearly 250 square miles of robotaxi coverage in 5 cities

Waymo is growing its driverless service area by nearly 250 square miles over the next week, spread across Los Angeles, Nashville, Orlando, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

That’s about as big as Tesla’s entire Houston Robotaxi geofence after this week’s expansion, and Waymo is adding it in cities where it already runs with nobody in the driver’s seat.

The company announced the expansion in a short post on its blog today. Here’s what changes in each market, with Waymo’s updated service area maps:

Service now runs down the coast into the South Bay, through Manhattan Beach and Redondo Beach to Torrance.

The zone pushes further south, and riders can now get to the zoo.

Coverage on the east side nearly doubles, and there’s more service downtown.

The service area now stretches north to La Jolla, taking in University City and Clairemont along the way.

Waymo is pushing further into the South Bay, including a connection to BART at Berryessa station in San Jose. The service area now runs from San Francisco down the Peninsula to San Jose and Campbell.

Waymo didn’t break out square mileage by city, and it didn’t say how many vehicles it’s adding to cover the new ground. The updated maps are already in the Waymo app.

Some of these markets are very young. Waymo opened Nashville to public riders in April with a zone of about 60 square miles covering downtown, Midtown, Music Row, and East Nashville. San Diego only went public on September 1, with roughly 50 square miles between the beach and I-15 that barely crossed north of I-8. So getting to La Jolla less than two months later is a big jump.

In May, Waymo pushed its coverage past 1,400 square miles across 11 cities, which is bigger than the state of Rhode Island. Since then, it went driverless in Las Vegas, launched San Diego, and now says it operates in 15 US metros with more than 500,000 paid rides per week. It’s even mapping Toronto for a 2028 launch.

Tesla is also drawing bigger maps. After launching Robotaxi in Dallas and Houston with tiny geofences in April, it stretched Houston to about 254 square miles this week, according to Robotaxi Tracker. But the tracker counts 34 vehicles in Houston.

I'd like to see Waymo add more airports to their service list. Airports are huge drivers of both ride count and revenue for ride services. Waymo currently serves airports in some of their cities, such as Phoenix, San Francisco, and Nashville. However, other major airports such as LAX, Atlanta, and Dallas/Fort Worth do not currently have terminal service even though Waymo operates in those cities. Adding these might not look flashy on a map, but it would be a huge addition to Waymo's bottom line.

And on the metric that reflects actual use, it’s not close. Waymo logged 3.9 million rider-only miles per week in Q2 2026, while Tesla’s driverless fleet did 558,000 miles in its latest reported week, mostly in Austin. That’s about 7x, and it comes on the same day Elon Musk claimed the robotaxi race against Waymo “was never a real contest.”

I like this. Good progress. But I’ll be truly impressed when the Bay Area service area extends south into LA, expands north, and the same happens in San Diego.

It’s going to happen. Waymo is already dabbling with highway operations in California.I can see them linking all those service areas within the next 2 years. Maybe even by the end of next year if all goes well.

#4877. Detached Nails More Than 4 Times Higher Among GLP-1 Users, Study Finds

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 users have reported various unusual side effects like “Ozempic feet,” “Ozempic butt,” and “Ozempic breasts.” These changes have been largely tied to rapid weight loss.

Now, fingernails have entered the conversation. Nails detaching from the nail bed or changing color may be more common among people taking GLP-1 drugs, according to a new study. In the study, which researchers presented in October at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026 in Vienna, people taking GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide — Ozempic, Wegovy — and tirzepatide — Mounjaro, Zepbound — reported nail detachment and nail discoloration more often than people who didn’t take the drugs.

When the researchers counted only nail changes that started after treatment began, the link between GLP-1 use and nail detachment nearly disappeared, study author Charles Taïeb, MD, PhD, told Healthline.

“This is why we insist that a substantial part of the nail excess reflects the patients’ overall health rather than the drug itself, while a modest drug-specific effect remains plausible,” Taïeb said.Earlier research has also linked GLP-1 use to hair loss. In the new study, the researchers explained why they examined nails, noting that nails and hair both grow from cells that divide quickly.

However, the researchers cautioned in a press release that the study can’t establish that the drugs caused the nail changes. Both the nail study and a companion hair study captured self-reported symptoms at a single point in time, a design that can identify associations only, they said.

For the study, researchers examined a representative sample of people in France, the United States, Brazil, and Mexico.

Participants included 575 people taking GLP-1 drugs and 1,329 people with type 2 diabetes, obesity, or both conditions, who had never taken GLP-1 drugs.

The average treatment duration was 18.5 months, and researchers tracked weight loss over three months.

They also looked separately at people who had lost weight, to help tell whether the drugs or the weight loss explained the changes. However, the abstract didn’t specify which GLP-1 drugs participants took.

The researchers have submitted the findings to peer-reviewed dermatology journals, where they are under review, Taïeb told Healthline. Here’s what they found.

According to the American Academy of Dermatology (AAD), nail detachment, or onycholysis, occurs when a nail lifts, and the lifted area often appears white.

Taïeb told Healthline that the study asked about “nail detachment” because patients, not doctors, filled out the questionnaire. Nail detachment was the strongest signal among the five nail changes the researchers asked about, Taïeb said.

According to the abstract, 39% of GLP-1 users reported nail separation or detachment (onycholysis), compared with 9% of nonusers.

Nail discoloration is a change in a nail’s usual color, such as white, yellow, or greenish-black, according to the AAD.According to the abstract, 46% of GLP-1 users reported discoloration, compared with 17% of nonusers. Ridges or grooves and fragile nails were also more common among GLP-1 users.

Mir B. Ali, MD, a bariatric surgeon and medical director of the MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Los Angeles, said that while he prescribes GLP-1s, nail detachment hasn’t come up in his practice. Ali wasn’t involved in the research.“I haven’t had anybody complain of that. It’s not something we really see,” he told Healthline. He said his patients more often mention brittle nails or minor changes in nail color.

Over a three-month period, 76% of GLP-1 users reported weight loss, compared with 47% of nonusers, according to the abstract.Weight loss alone didn’t appear to explain the nail findings, the researchers said in the press release. The differences between users and nonusers held up when they looked only at people who had lost weight.The researchers also cautioned in the press release that the study can’t show the drugs caused the changes. They noted that about half of GLP-1 users had nail problems before starting treatment.

Adjusting for skin conditions and nutritional deficiencies weakened some of the associations, they said, though nail detachment and discoloration stayed about two to three times as common among users.Those adjustments relied on conditions participants reported, including iron, vitamin B12, zinc, and vitamin D deficiencies, as well as psoriasis, eczema, and other skin conditions, Taïeb said.“GLP-1 medications may affect the nails indirectly rather than directly,” said Tanya Evans, MD, a board certified dermatologist and medical director of the Skin Cancer Program at the Melanoma Clinic at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, who wasn’t involved in the research.Because the drugs reduce appetite, some people may eat less protein, iron, and zinc, which can contribute to brittle nails, discoloration, or nail detachment, Evans told Healthline. Rapid weight loss may also temporarily disrupt nail growth, much as it can trigger hair shedding, she said.Ali said the total amount of weight a person loses plays a bigger role in hair and nail changes than the rate at which they lose it.

The U.S. labels for Wegovy and Zepbound list hair loss as a side effect reported in clinical trials.

The labels for the Ozempic, both injectable and pill form, as well as Mounjaro, list hair loss as a side effect, based on reports received after the drugs entered the market. Those reports don’t establish how often it happens or whether the drugs caused it.

As such, researchers have been examining GLP-1-related hair loss.

A companion study of the same participants found hair and scalp changes were also more common among GLP-1 users, according to that study’s abstract, also provided to Healthline:

Scalp redness was about three times as common among users, and most users with hair loss also had scalp symptoms such as itching, redness, or scaling.Scalp inflammation may play a role in hair changes among GLP-1 users, in addition to the shedding that often follows rapid weight loss, one of the study’s authors stated in the news release.“This raises the possibility that inflammation may be contributing in some patients, rather than the problem being solely the classic temporary hair shedding associated with rapid weight loss,” Evans said.Experts have told Healthline that hair loss on GLP-1 drugs is often temporary and tied to weight loss.“Hair loss, we see commonly, not only in patients who are on GLP-1 medications, but also in our surgical weight loss patients,” Ali said.

“When you lose weight, especially in women, it releases hormones. You’re getting metabolic changes, and all these things can lead to hair loss and some changes in the nails.” Ali said he tells patients that “as the weight stabilizes at a healthy weight, the hormones stabilize and the hair tends to come back to where it was before.”

Nail detachment and discoloration don’t appear as adverse reactions in the current U.S. prescribing information for Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, or Zepbound.

Ali said the best thing patients can do is get the right nutrition, including enough protein. He said he also advises patients to take a multivitamin along with B-complex, vitamin D, and calcium.

“I would not recommend stopping the GLP-1 medication simply because nail detachment occurs,” Evans said. She advised people to tell their doctor about any new changes in hair, scalp, or nails.Treatment for nail detachment or discoloration depends on the cause, Evans said. A dermatologist can check for an infection, an inflammatory nail disorder, a nutritional problem, an injury, or another explanation, she said.A detached nail recovers as a new nail grows out from its base, Evans said. That takes about 4 to 6 months for a fingernail and 9 to 12 months for a toenail.

Lastly, the AAD recommends having a board certified dermatologist examine any nail that’s lifting.

The AAD also recommends seeing a dermatologist if skin, hair, or nail side effects don’t improve, as they can help determine whether symptoms are due to the medication or another condition.“The important message is don’t panic, but don’t ignore persistent nail changes either,” Evans said.
