#4776. Someone ran Rivian’s pedal-by-wire e-bike out of battery and things got weird

The ALSO TM-B is one of the most technologically interesting new e-bikes to hit the road in years, largely because it does away with one of the most fundamental parts of a bicycle: the mechanical connection between the pedals and rear wheel. With only copper wires connecting the pedals to the rear wheel, the TM-B is one of the most revolutionary new e-bikes in years.

But that raises an obvious question. What happens when the battery dies?

One early Launch Edition owner, Aaron Draczynski, decided to find out by deliberately running his TM-B down toward empty to see whether ALSO’s drive-by-wire system would leave him stranded.

He shared the experience on YouTube, discovering that the answer is surprisingly complicated – and involves something called “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Unlike a conventional e-bike, where the rider’s pedaling mechanically turns the rear wheel through a chain or belt, the ALSO TM-B uses a pedal-by-wire drivetrain. Pedaling generates electricity, while the rear wheel is driven electrically.

That arrangement enables all sorts of interesting features, including electronically simulated gearing and the Launch Edition’s massive Level 10 boost mode, which can multiply rider input by up to 10 times.

But it also means there’s no traditional drivetrain to fall back on when the battery runs out.

Fortunately, the bike doesn’t simply go from full power to dead.

The owner began his experiment at 31% charge and quickly watched the bike progressively restrict its maximum assist as the battery drained closer to empty. From 23% to 13%, the maximum boost dropped from Level 8 to Level 5 as it began conserving battery.

By 10% charge, the bike was limited to Level 4. At 8%, it dropped to Level 3, followed by Level 2 at 5%. Shortly afterward, only Level 1 remained. Then at 4% battery, conventional electric assistance disappeared entirely.

Interestingly, the normal electronic shifting of the bike’s simulated software gears continued to work through most of that process. But when the battery reached 4%, things changed as the bike started exhibiting issues. The first sign of trouble came when the bike began seemingly randomly shifting gears while in manual mode without the rider even touching the shifter. Several times per second, the bike seemed to want to shift itself between gears.

Keep in mind that the TM-B doesn’t have actual physical gears (and no chain or derailleur, for that matter), but instead simulates various gears using predefined software to make the rider feel like they are working more or less intensely to pedal the bike.

Once the TM-B reached its final low-battery state, an infinity symbol appeared on the display and the bike entered what the owner referred to as “Infinite Turtle Mode.”

Instead of using stored battery energy to provide meaningful assistance, the system effectively attempts to pass the rider’s pedaling energy through the electronic drivetrain to keep the rear wheel turning. It’s similar in concept to those old crank-powered flashlights, which, even with a dead storage battery, would still illuminate for as long as the owner cranked them.

And on flat ground, the owner reported that the infinite turtle mode apparently worked surprisingly well.

Draczynski described the experience as roughly equivalent to pedaling a normal bicycle in fourth gear. There was resistance at the pedals, and he could maintain a reasonable pace without feeling like he was simply spinning his legs uselessly.

Then he reached a hill and found the limitation of that effectiveness. Even a slight incline transformed the experience, with the bike feeling more like it was permanently stuck in seventh or eighth gear. Getting home through his hilly neighborhood became, in his words, a “truly grueling ordeal.”

Manual shifting was also disabled in this mode, meaning there was no way to electronically select an easier virtual gear for climbing, since again, there aren’t any physical gears in the bike. Everything in the pedaling experience is software-simulated.

That’s an important limitation for a bike relying entirely on a drive-by-wire drivetrain. The infinite turtle mode might keep you moving with significant effort on level terrain, but it doesn’t turn a dead TM-B into a conventional bicycle, unless that conventional bicycle is being ridden through beach sand.

The low-power state apparently shuts down some other features as well. The owner could no longer lock or unlock the TM-B through ALSO’s smartphone app, though he did report the bike’s touchscreen controls continued working, and he guessed that the bike had shut down connectivity to conserve power for its key systems to operate.

Perhaps more concerning than the low-battery riding experience was what happened when this particular TM-B was simply sitting in the owner’s garage.

Describing another scenario he encountered, Draczynski says he left the bike sitting unplugged in his garage at around 70% charge. The following evening, it had fallen to 40%, and a day later it was down to 18%.

When he returned the next morning, the TM-B displayed a “Bike issue detected” message followed by “Install battery to ride.”

There was just one problem: the battery was already installed.

Plugging in the charger didn’t initially help because the bike apparently couldn’t detect its own battery, and thus charging didn’t begin. Worse, the battery refused to eject using the normal ejection process, leaving the owner unable to remove it and charge it off of the bike.

Ultimately, Draczynski used the physical reset button underneath the frame, which brought the system back to life. The bike recognized the battery again and began charging normally.

Much like modern EVs, I would imagine a lot of these issues will be fixed via a software update. Early adoption is fun but you’re basically beta testing a product for the company at full price.

That degree of overnight battery drain obviously isn’t something we’d expect from a normal e-bike, so hopefully this was either an isolated software issue or something ALSO can address with an update. For his part, Draczynski suspects that the bike might be draining its battery so heavily at rest due to the lack of a cell signal in his garage. “I was quite surprised at the drop from day to day,” he explained on Reddit. “If I had to wager a guess, the bike might be searching for a cellular signal, but there’s no reception in my garage so it’s just draining the battery.”

But the experiment offers an interesting first real-world look at one of the biggest questions surrounding ALSO’s unusual drivetrain.

A normal e-bike with a dead battery becomes a heavy bicycle. The TM-B instead becomes something much stranger: an electricity-generating exercise machine that uses your legs to generate current, electronically sends that current through the bike, and then uses it to turn the rear wheel.

And based on this testing, it does in fact work. Just try not to be at the bottom of a hill when you find out for yourself.

#4775. The First Hit: Why You Shouldn't Wait for a Second

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 5, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

Imagine having an argument with your partner. Emotions are high, voices are raised, arms are flailing, and then they hit you. The “hit” isn’t hard enough to leave a bruise or mark. It’s not hard enough to knock you off your feet. In fact, it’s just a slight sting that dissipates in seconds. It’s just hard enough to get your attention.

In that moment, the conversation stops, in large part because you are so shocked. Later, your partner says that it wasn’t really a hit; it was more of a “warning tap.” It was only used to get you to “shut up and listen.”

When physical aggression is disguised as a “warning,” the bigger issue becomes our act of minimizing it.

Any “tap” delivered in anger to control, intimidate, or punish you is not a warning. It’s violence. Just because you call an apple a desk doesn’t mean that the apple automatically stops having the characteristics of an apple. No matter what you call it, an apple is an apple. And no matter what you call it, using physical aggression to intimidate, punish, or control your partner is violence. Calling it a “warning tap” doesn’t change what it is.

Think about how warnings work. When a fire alarm sounds, it’s a warning that the room could fill with smoke soon. When a teenager breaks curfew and they get a warning, the next step is typically a punishment. When a police officer gives you a warning, it means the next time could be a ticket.

Warnings are typically a sign that, if you don’t change course, the situation will escalate or intensify. So, when a partner resorts to a “warning tap,” isn’t the message that the situation will get worse if you don’t stop?

Your challenge comes with physical consequences.

While we cannot automatically know our partner's intentions, we should question why physical aggression was introduced into the disagreement in the first place. Regardless of the intention, the message is troubling: physical force has now become part of the relationship's conflict. Research on coercive control suggests that intimate partner violence is not always about the physical act itself. Sometimes, aggression is part of a broader pattern of intimidation, dominance, and control (Myhill, 2015). In these situations, the impact of violence extends beyond physical injury. It can also influence how safe someone feels expressing disagreement or asserting their independence.

Throughout my career as a clinical psychologist, I have encountered women who describe the first incident of physical violence. Frequently, that first incident is followed by tears, apologies, begging, promises, and gifts. Sometimes, it’s even followed by changed behavior…temporarily.

"He's never done anything like that before."

"He apologized and promised it would never happen again."

The absence of serious injury or pain does not mean the absence of serious risk. Research on intimate partner violence is clear. A history of violence in a relationship is a risk factor for future violence. Spencer and Stith (2020) examined risk factors associated with intimate partner homicide and found that factors such as previous physical violence, threats, and controlling behaviors were relevant to understanding lethal risk.

This does not mean that every first hit will inevitably lead to a second hit or that every aggressive partner will eventually commit homicide. However, violence in a relationship should not be dismissed just because it hasn’t happened before. In other words, take the first hit seriously.

October was Domestic Violence Awareness Month, but awareness shouldn't end when the calendar changes. It means very little if we continue to normalize the early behaviors that may signal danger. Do you need a broken bone, black eye, bruises, or chipped teeth before you acknowledge something is wrong?

When the fire alarm goes off, we don’t wait to see fire before we make a move. We recognize the warning and take it seriously. The same rule applies to violence in your relationship.

They don’t get a free pass because they haven’t done it previously. It still matters even if it didn’t leave a mark. It’s not harmless because we are calling it a “warning tap” instead of what it is, which is violence.

Keep in mind that leaving a violent relationship can be dangerous, particularly when there is a history of threats or controlling behavior. If you are experiencing intimate partner violence, developing a safety plan and identifying trusted sources of support are important steps toward protecting yourself.

The important question isn't whether the "tap" hurt but why your partner believed that putting their hands on you was an acceptable response to a disagreement.

And if they insist that it was only a warning, perhaps it's time to ask the question you may have been avoiding all along: A warning of what, exactly?

Myhill, A. (2015). Measuring coercive control: What can we learn from national population surveys? Violence Against Women, 21(3), 355–375. doi.org/10.1177/1077801214568032

Spencer, C. M., & Stith, S. M. (2020). Risk factors for male perpetration and female victimization of intimate partner homicide: A meta-analysis. Trauma, Violence, & Abuse, 21(3), 527–540. doi.org/10.1177/1524838018781101

#4774. Harley-Davidson’s electric motorcycle brand LiveWire warns it may not survive

Harley-Davidson-born electric motorcycle maker LiveWire has issued a troubling warning about its financial future, announcing that it has substantial doubt about its ability to continue operating as a going concern. The news sent LiveWire’s stock plunging more than 40% on Thursday morning as the company withdrew its full-year financial guidance.

The announcement comes despite some signs of improving sales, with LiveWire reporting a 38% increase in third-quarter revenue to $7.9 million and a 21% rise in motorcycle unit sales. However, the company continues to burn through cash, reporting a net loss of $18.6 million for the quarter.

LiveWire’s cash reserves have also dwindled significantly, falling from $82.8 million at the end of 2025 to just $39.9 million as of September 30, 2026.

The company has now formed a special restructuring committee to explore potential financing arrangements, strategic partnerships, investments, or even a sale. It also withdrew its previous guidance projecting a $70 million to $80 million operating loss for 2026.

The financial warning comes at a particularly pivotal moment for LiveWire, which is preparing to launch its most affordable electric motorcycles yet.

The upcoming LiveWire S4 Honcho series represents a major departure from the company’s existing premium electric motorcycles, offering smaller, lighter, and significantly more affordable models designed to attract a much broader audience of riders with a starting price below US $5,000.

The lower prices could dramatically increase LiveWire’s sales volumes, especially as the company attempts to move beyond the relatively small market for high-dollar electric motorcycles. The Honcho lineup is also expected to help lower the barrier to entry for new riders, with approachable electric motorcycles that eliminate the complexity of clutch and gear shifting.

LiveWire is also preparing to showcase its latest developments at EICMA in Milan next week, where it is expected to display new models and further expand its upcoming electric motorcycle lineup.

Whether those new motorcycles can arrive quickly enough to turn around the company’s financial situation remains to be seen.

This is genuinely sad news to see. If there’s any legacy motorcycle manufacturer that deserves to succeed in the electric motorcycle space, it’s Harley-Davidson.

Make all the jokes you want about old dudes in leather jackets riding around on loud, chrome-covered motorcycles. But the fact is that Harley-Davidson was taking electric motorcycles seriously when most other major motorcycle manufacturers were still pretending they didn’t exist.

Harley-Davidson didn’t just dip its toes into electric motorcycles. It dove in headfirst, developing the original LiveWire electric motorcycle well over a decade ago and eventually bringing a highly acclaimed production bike to market in 2019. That’s right, Harley-Davidson had a legitimately impressive electric motorcycle on the road before COVID was even a thing. Meanwhile, most of its legacy competitors are only now starting to roll out their first serious electric offerings.

Maybe it's news to Electrek, but while Harley was contemplating electric motorcycles, Zero was selling them for over a decade and continues to do so. There are some high end bikes that Livewire just didn't compete with yet cost $30k when it first came out damaging the brand perception. Newer, lower priced models don't help.

There is also competition from run around eScooters that are way cheaper even cheaper than upcoming Honcho.

And that’s what makes this so frustrating. Harley-Davidson did the hard part. It invested early, developed excellent technology, received rave reviews, and proved that electric motorcycles could be thrilling, premium machines. But building great motorcycles and building a profitable electric motorcycle business have turned out to be two very different challenges.

The timing is especially unfortunate because I genuinely believe LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho series could be exactly what the company needs. These smaller, significantly more affordable electric motorcycles could finally open LiveWire up to a younger audience that doesn’t have $15,000 to drop on a flagship motorcycle but still wants something fun, stylish, and electric for $5,000.

In many ways, that audience seems like a much more natural fit for LiveWire’s branding and ethos than the premium motorcycle market it has been chasing for years.

I really hope LiveWire can find what it needs to get through this difficult period. After spending more than a decade helping drag the legacy motorcycle industry kicking and screaming into the electric age, it would be a real shame to see the company stumble just as its most promising chapter might be about to begin.

#4773. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4772. Jasion Poki review: The Electric Minibike that packs heavy-duty fun

In our transportation reporting, we rarely come across something as fun as today’s review of the Jasion Poki.

The Poki is a severely overpowered electric minibike that looks like it came from yesteryear. If the power isn’t enough, it also packs some cool tricks, and we’re not (just) talking about wheelies this time.

So taking a look at this bad boy, it just screams fun. It is really low to the ground, has a big, wide seat large enough for 2 people as long as they are under 350lbs total, and has pegs for 2 people and a basket, great for carrying a picnic and an extra helmet.

This thing is built like a tank, and it tips the scales accordingly. Getting this thing in my SUV ruptured a few discs in my back, though its compact nature means it fit quite well. Loosen the handlebars and it is downright compact. But that weight is strangely like 50lbs heavier than I would expect at close to 140lbs.

That also makes the built-in wheelies a little bit more suspect. My son, who is by now becoming an expert at wheelies, found this one to be a bit more difficult than the auto wheelies on bikes like the Anyland or new Yozma IN11.

OK so not only does this little powerhouse get you (and your friend) around town in style and it also makes wheelies a bit easier; but it also has a huge Bluetooth speaker in the back that sounds like a Harley and is all synced up with the actual controller so it sounds real.

Sure, it is a gimmick, but it is a fun one, and it might actually make the low-down bike a little safer since it is going to be out of the sight of most cars.

I love this thing. It is my favorite bike to go to the beach on (and it does well in the sand with those fat tires). But I think there are some big misses here. First of all, it has no business going over 40mph. Not only does it feel scary with those tiny wheels, but speed wobbles puts both the rider a possible second rider at significant risk here. This is a fun bike and it should top out at 20-28mph max. Keep all the torque, just cut out the power at a reasonable top speed.

Also it should weigh a lot less. At 140lbs, it is silly hard to get into the back of a car, which it easily fits in. Making the frame aluminum would go a long way here. Also, if this thing rolled on top of you, it would be a bad day.

Make this thing safer and more portable, and I’d recommend everyone with a beach commute to get one. As it stands, best for responsible adults with strong backs and a Peter Pan complex.

The Poki is currently priced at $1,799, and customers can get 5% off with the code Electrek.

#4771. A Simple, Heartwarming Way to Get Out of Your Own Head

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 5, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

There is no shortage of influencers out there providing advice and hawking products to improve our lives. So, whether it is how to maximize fitness gains, how to sleep better, or how and when to meditate, we are seemingly all on a quest to feel happier. Yet, what if there's another way to feel better that we may not think about enough?

Here's a newsflash: If you want to really move the feel-better needle, then help someone else. You don't have to do huge things to help others. I’m saying the more we notice people who could use something from us, the more it can positively change our moods, especially if we act on that urge to help them.

There are endless videos online of people doing kind things for strangers, including paying for gas, cleaning up yards, and providing money to those in need. These stories are heartwarming. But what if we are watching popular videos about kindness and not enough understanding the power of doing kind things ourselves? Do we want to settle for those vicarious doses of feeling moved by the kind actions taken by others and then just call it a day?

In my new book, Help Them: And Watch Your Own Life Get Better, I further discuss the powerful emotional health benefits we gain by directly helping others. Maybe someone you know could really feel good getting a phone call. Is someone you know going through a tough time and could really perk up with some encouragement? Or, and this is tough for all of us, maybe somebody needs the wonderful gift of you "just listening" without immediately jumping in with advice.

I don’t know about you, but for years I've been internally preoccupied (OK, I’ll admit it—often consumed) by my own thoughts. It seems to me, the questions that really weigh on all of us are things like: Am I really happy? Or, did I mess that up? And, of course, we go down "Regret Alley" with thoughts like, “If only I didn't mess that up, I'd be so much better off.” That said, do you agree that there is a point where self-focus becomes its own trap?

By helping others, at least for a while, you are thinking about something besides yourself. This notion is supported by research on kindness and helping behavior that has linked helping others with our own greater well-being. How about right now, you get back in touch with a time when you knew you made a difference? Didn’t it feel pretty darn good? Next, let's look at how to keep helping helpful versus it ever becoming harmful.

Like most things in life, there can be too much done sometimes when it comes to helping others. I have seen this play out with many of my parent-coaching clients, for whom helping is not always healthy. Specifically, I see this all the time with parents of struggling adult children: A parent pays another bill, makes another phone call, fixes another problem, or bails their child out of another mess.

The danger is that sometimes helping becomes rescuing. Sadly, and I will even say tragically, rescuing can keep another person from developing the skills they need. So the more useful question is not "How can I help?" but "Will my help actually help?" In some cases, giving support may be best through giving our listening ear than giving from our wallets. Further, sometimes we may help best if, after weighing the situation, we say no.

When it comes to our perceptions of what helping is, we tend to think meaningful acts have to be dramatic. But they don't have to be huge acts of kindness. How about you send that text you've been loosely debating sending to someone who may feel really good about hearing from you? Better yet, call them and let them hear your supportive voice. While you're at it, maybe tell that person why you really appreciate them.

It feels good to share that a teen counseling client of mine just told me the other day how great he felt by helping an elderly neighbor who had recently lost her husband of 40 years by raking some leaves; he politely refused her offer to pay him. A parent I work with recently shared how good she felt about becoming more patient with her children when they would go into their long, colorful stories.

I hope this post inspires you to help others because it may turn out to be the best self-improvement plan you could ever embark on. When you do help others, you will feel less in your head because your focus has meaningfully shifted. The more we help others, the better we feel. So, please: Help them.

#4769. RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

“The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.

#4768. Unknown bald eagle spotted on Shadow’s nest

Published Oct 27, 2026 4:18 PM EDT

The bald eagle nest in Big Bear Valley has welcomed a new visitor. On Tuesday, cameras spotted an unknown adult spending time in the nest once shared by Jackie and Shadow.

The new eagle was first seen last week, but returned on Tuesday for about 30 minutes to fiddle with a few sticks and pose in front of the nest cam operated by Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV). A sub-adult eagle has also been spotted on FOBBV’s cameras in recent weeks. Shadow has not been seen by the cameras since October 23. Kaydee, a young adult bald eagle who has been seen arranging sticks and singing with Shadow in the past few months, was last seen on October 21.

It’s not unusual for bald eagles to spend less time in their nests in the fall. Fans often refer to this time as “bald eagle vacation,” where the birds will spend time exploring other parts of the area and sleeping in trees with more cover. Mating season for the Big Bear Valley bald eagles typically starts in December. It’s not yet known if Shadow will return to his nest or mate with a new partner following the death of Jackie on August 10.

Jackie and Shadow were not the original inhabitants of the nest seen on the FOBBV cams. Jackie’s parents, Lucy and Ricky, built the nest during the 2012-2013 nesting season. Shortly after the 2011-2012 nesting season, when Jackie was born and eventually fledged, Lucy and Ricky’s old nest blew away in a strong storm.

The old nest sat at the top of a dead tree. The new nest occupied a nearby, stronger tree about 50 feet away from where Jackie was raised. Lucy and Ricky abandoned the nest in the 2015-2016 season, opting instead to build a new nest nearby. At the beginning of the 2016-2017 nesting season, Lucy and Ricky disappeared from the area. It’s unknown where they went or what happened to them. But that same season, a juvenile female began hanging out at their old pad. Experts later guessed this was Jackie. She used this nest, first with original partner Mr. B and later with Shadow, until her death.

In summer 2026, Shadow continued to tend to the nest with the pair’s chicks, Sandy and Luna, until they fledged in mid-July. In the months that followed, he continued to visit the nest and eventually allowed Kaydee to also spend time there.

Stay tuned to the FOBBV cameras to see how this bald eagle story continues to unfold. Camera 1 (the main nest cam) is currently running its usual 24/7 streaming schedule, but Camera 2 (the wide angle) is currently being turned off at night to conserve energy.

#4767. Core Ethical Values for College Students

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 5, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

“We all do better when we all do better,” according to Paul Wellstone, one of my college professors and a former U.S. senator. These are times of uncertainty, volatility, lack of standards in our leaders, and national strife—just to name a few. Having an internal ethical compass can only help college students, the campus community, and society as a whole.

Besides being beneficial for the people around us, living in alignment with our chosen values is good for our mental health in many ways. Acting with integrity gives us a sense of meaning and purpose, often found to be core aspects of both mental and physical health. Treating others well can release positive neurochemicals like serotonin, endorphins, and dopamine, which boost mood and lower stress, as well as foster authentic relationships, an essential part of well-being.

Offered here is an introductory list of ethical values for college student that borrows from commonly-held ethical systems from a variety of sources and professions. These are aspirational ideals, meant as ethical considerations students may take to enhance their own ethical code.

Integrity: Being committed to doing what's right and staying consistent with your moral principles, even when no one is watching, is the core of integrity. It takes courage to choose what might be an unpopular or difficult position.

Honesty: Nearly every ethical code includes this. Honesty is telling the truth as we believe it to be, without trying to deceive or mislead others.

Care: The minimum requirement for care is to do no harm, but we can elevate that to acting to relieve the pain of others. Care also involves treating ourselves with the same physical, mental, and psychological compassion.

Respect: Both in person and online, respect is about valuing the inherent worth and dignity of others and treating them with basic human decency. This follows the near-universal principle of the Golden Rule (treating others how you would like to be treated) or the Platinum Rule (treating others how they would prefer to be treated).

Responsibility: A responsible person is reliable, keeps commitments, and understands that our actions affect more than just ourselves.

Accountability: Accountability starts by being willing to be held accountable for mistakes and being willing to fix them instead of blaming others.

Humility: Humility is recognizing that we still have a lot to learn, we might not always be right, and that we are willing and open to learning new things.

I believe that the overall wellness of college students—for whom it is developmentally appropriate to be in the process of building their identities—can benefit from having a road map that influences how they treat others and navigate ethical dilemmas in their personal and professional lives. It takes some practice to bring ethical reflection to decision-making, but the positive results can be transformational.

Boreham ID, Schutte NS. The relationship between purpose in life and depression and anxiety: A meta-analysis. J Clin Psychol. 2023 Dec;79(12):2736-2767.

Novak, L., Malinakova, K., Mikoska, P., van Dijk, J. P., & Tavel, P. (2022). Neural correlates of compassion: An integrative systematic review. International Journal of Psychophysiology, 172, 46–59.

#4766. Waymo picks Toyota bZ4X as its next robotaxi, starting in Japan in 2027

Waymo is adding the Toyota bZ4X to its robotaxi lineup. Toyota will build a custom version of the electric SUV with the Waymo Driver integrated right on the line in Japan, and a test fleet will start operating there in 2027.

It’s the first actual vehicle to come out of the partnership the two companies signed last year. And it gives Waymo a Japanese-built car for its Tokyo launch, with the UK and other markets to follow.

When Waymo and Toyota first announced their deal in April 2025, it was a preliminary agreement to “explore” working together on autonomous driving, including in personally owned vehicles. Lots of intent, no product.

Now there’s a product. According to Waymo’s announcement, Toyota will produce the vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, and Waymo’s self-driving hardware will be installed and integrated at that same site instead of being retrofitted somewhere else.

The robotaxi bZ4X gets a few rider-focused changes: extra rear legroom, automatic doors, a power liftgate, and ambient lighting. Waymo didn’t share sensor specs, unit volumes, or what each vehicle costs.

Operations in 2027 are about testing and validating the autonomous bZ4X fleet in Japan. The UK and “other Waymo markets” come in later years, with no dates attached.

The two companies also say they’ll keep working on autonomous tech for Toyota’s personal vehicles, plus safety projects with Woven by Toyota, the automaker’s software arm.

Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov said that “Toyota’s commitment to zero traffic accidents resonates deeply with us at Waymo.”

The timing lines up with Waymo’s Japan plans. In September, Waymo said it’s targeting fully driverless commercial rides in Tokyo in 2027 with taxi operator Nihon Kotsu and ride-hailing app GO, scaling to about 100 vehicles, pending regulatory approval.

In the US, Waymo’s fleet is still mostly made up of Jaguar I-Pace SUVs, a model Jaguar no longer produces. It’s been adding the Zeekr-built Ojai van and the Hyundai Ioniq 5, and Hyundai is reportedly in talks to supply up to 50,000 Ioniq 5 robotaxis by 2028.

The bZ4X makes four. It isn’t Toyota’s first robotaxi bZ4X either: Toyota and Pony.ai started mass-producing bZ4X-based robotaxis in China earlier this year.

For US readers, the refreshed model is sold here simply as the Toyota bZ, starting at $34,900. A cheap, high-volume base vehicle matters a lot when you’re trying to scale a fleet.

And Waymo is scaling. It now does over 500,000 paid rides a week across 15 US metros, and it picked Toronto as its first Canadian city earlier this month, with riders targeted for 2028.

This is a big one, even if the bZ4X is about as exciting as a toaster.

Waymo’s biggest constraint right now is cars. It has been running a fleet built on a discontinued Jaguar, and every new automaker it signs adds manufacturing capacity it doesn’t have to build itself. Toyota is the world’s best-selling automaker. Having it build Waymo-ready vehicles on its own assembly line is exactly the kind of industrial partner Waymo needed.

If Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning a personal vehicle, they are likely working on it. It doesn’t mean that it is going to happen but it’s obviously an avenue that they are both willing to explore. If things work out and they are actually able to bring a fully autonomous vehicle to market, that’s an extremely significant advantage from a top legacy car manufacturer that ultimately changes the game for Toyota and could potentially put them in the middle of the competition with other EV manufacturers.

Yes, the bZ4X had a rough start (Toyota recalled the first batch in 2022 because the wheels could come off). But it has come a long way now – becoming boring and reliable. And for a robotaxi, boring and reliable is the whole point.

Compare that with Tesla’s approach: a two-seat Cybercab with no steering wheel, built in-house, with a self-certified autonomy stack that still isn’t operating at anything close to Waymo’s scale. Waymo keeps plugging its driver into existing EVs from established automakers and expanding city by city. So far, that’s working.

The way it is looking now. It sounds like Toyota will take over manufacturing Waymo driver cars for right-hand-drive markets. But what interests me most is the personal-vehicle angle. Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning it, but there’s still nothing concrete. If Toyota actually puts the Waymo Driver in a car you can buy, Tesla’s FSD Supervised pitch gets a lot harder to sell. Will that happen before the end of the decade? Who knows.

#4765. 9 nature-inspired pumpkin carving patterns from the National Park Service

Published Oct 28, 2026 9:48 AM EDT

The approaching All Hallows Eve means the time has come to carve that jack-o’-lantern to light the way for trick-or-treaters or keep the bad spirits away. The National Park Service’s Pumpkin Carving Challenge offers gourd enthusiasts a way to celebrate nature’s spooky side.

“Nothing says ‘scary’ quite like a 2,000-pound furry mammal you’ve annoyed launching you into another dimension. Or the tree above. Either way, it comes with a thud. Talk about a smashing Halloween,” the NPS writes.

Carvers can choose from nine templates that can be used to craft a more off-the-beaten-path jack o’lantern. Templates include pictures of bats, spooky spiderwebs, and (our favorite), fat bears.

The Batty One celebrates one of Halloween’s most enduring symbols. National parks serve as  roosting grounds or migratory stops for millions of bats all year round, not just during spooky season.

The Close Encounter offers a cautionary tale. Please view animals from a safe distance for their safety and yours. One visitor to Yellowstone National Park certainly learned that in July.

The Autumn Leaves pays tribute to the spectacular display of color trees shown during the fall. And what could be more autumnal than leaf peeping in a national park?

The Full Moon is a template that will “eclipse” the others, according to the NPS. Wolves currently roam in at least six national parks.

The Camper is for those of us who love a good ghost story around a cracking camp fire.

The Fat Bear. Need we say more? Bring the Fat Bear Week fun right into Halloween with this template.

The Web Designer honors nature’s web slingers. The NPS even offers helpful tips on how to avoid the horror of walking into a spider web.

Pictures can be added to a growing digital pumpkin patch on social media using #FindYourPark or #EncuentraTuParque.

Some other ways to spice up your pumpkin creations this year include oozing pumpkins, using a vape to create a spooky smoke effect, and using kelp to make kelp-o’-lanterns.

#4764. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.
